questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Features and consequences of a merit rule
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a merit rule fixes about the selection procedure
questions.stem: An architect's brief for a civic complex notes that appointments to the design review panel are made by open examination rather than by nomination from serving officials.

options.text: A merit rule separates selection from patronage, so candidates are judged on the published test alone
A merit rule is decorative, since examiners can be influenced by the officials who administer the test
options.misconception: assumes administration of an exam decides the outcome

options.text: A merit rule works only where a school certificate is required, since formal qualification is the point
options.misconception: reduces merit to a formal qualification

options.text: A merit rule prevents nepotism entirely, so no related appointment can occur once it is introduced
options.misconception: claims a rule removes the underlying relationships

questions.explanation: A merit rule fixes the selection procedure in advance, so entry depends on the published test rather than connections. That makes the process auditable, which is what checks patronage.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule fixes before selection begins.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what state capacity means in terms of reach and delivery
questions.stem: A brief table records how much of a regional administration reaches its citizens: identity registration covers 9,600 of 12,000 households, and clinic delivery covers 84 per cent of settlements.

options.text: The administration has high capacity, because identity registration reaches four fifths of households
options.misconception: judges capacity by one administrative task alone

options.text: Capacity here is the administration's reach and its ability to deliver, measured on different services
The administration has high capacity, because clinic coverage of 84 per cent exceeds the registration figure
options.misconception: compares two service coverages as if they were one measure

options.text: The administration has low capacity, because no service reaches every household or settlement
options.misconception: demands universal coverage before granting capacity

questions.explanation: State capacity is the ability to reach citizens and deliver reliably, assessed across functions. The two figures measure different services, so they cannot be added or ranked against each other.
questions.hint: Ask what the two rows each measure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Fiscal capacity and the tax ratio
questions.learningObjective: Assess fiscal capacity from a tax ratio alongside the cost of borrowing
questions.stem: An architect's brief on a public library notes that the district collects 8.4 per cent of its economic output in tax and faces difficulty borrowing at reasonable rates.

options.text: Fiscal capacity is high, because a tax ratio above eight per cent shows a strong revenue base
options.misconception: treats one threshold as the measure of fiscal capacity

options.text: Fiscal capacity is high, because the district can still borrow, so its revenue position is secure
options.misconception: treats access to borrowing as evidence of fiscal strength

options.text: Fiscal capacity is limited, since a low tax ratio and costly borrowing both point to weak revenue power
Fiscal capacity is unrelated to the tax ratio, which describes only the mix of revenue sources
options.misconception: denies that the tax ratio bears on revenue power

questions.explanation: Fiscal capacity is the ability to raise and spend reliably. A low tax ratio with expensive borrowing suggests the base and lenders' confidence are weak, so the state's room to act is narrow.
questions.hint: Ask what both signals say about revenue power.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate revenue effort as revenue divided by the estimated tax base
questions.stem: An architect's brief on the region's finances records tax revenue of 2,400,000 units against an estimated tax base of 20,000,000 units. What is the revenue effort as a percentage of the base?
questions.explanation: Revenue effort is revenue divided by the tax base, so 2,400,000 over 20,000,000 is 0.12, that is 12 per cent. It is meaningful only alongside its base, since a larger base would lower the same revenue.
questions.hint: Divide revenue by the estimated tax base.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Argue that tax compliance rests on morale and not only on penalties
questions.stem: The architect's brief must explain to a municipal partner why tax compliance cannot be built only by adding penalties.

options.text: Because penalties must be set very high to have any effect on behaviour at all
options.misconception: assumes penalties work only when severe

options.text: Because taxpayers are already overburdened and would welcome firmer enforcement
options.misconception: assumes the main problem is the tax level

options.text: Because penalties are too expensive for the administration to administer
options.misconception: blames administrative cost rather than compliance

options.text: Because morale shapes willingness to pay, and a system people regard as fair is easier to enforce

questions.explanation: Tax morale is the willingness to pay what is owed, shaped by fairness and by whether others are seen to pay. Enforcement works better where that willingness exists, so penalties alone leave the cause untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what makes people willing to pay without a threat.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the compliance gap and read it against evidence of evasion

stimulus.body: For the district's vehicle registration duty we compare two figures for the same year. The tax due on the 30,000 registered vehicles was 6,900,000 units. The revenue actually collected was 5,850,000 units. The registration office reports 26,400 vehicles as renewed on time. A separate sample of 400 vehicles was inspected at the roadside, and 61 of them carried no current receipt. The office has not published a collection target for this year.

questions.stem: An architect's brief on the district's vehicle duty sets out the figures below.

options.text: The compliance gap is 1,050,000 units, and the road sample suggests much of it is deliberate evasion
The compliance gap is 6,900,000 units, because that is the total amount the duty would raise
options.misconception: counts the full liability as the gap

options.text: The compliance gap is 15 per cent, because one vehicle in seven was found without a receipt
options.misconception: equates a roadside sample rate with the revenue gap

options.text: There is no compliance gap, because 26,400 of 30,000 vehicles renewed on time as required
options.misconception: reads a high compliance count as full collection

questions.explanation: The gap is tax due minus tax collected: 6,900,000 minus 5,850,000, which is 1,050,000. The roadside sample of unreceipted vehicles suggests deliberate non-payment rather than administrative delay.
questions.hint: Subtract revenue collected from tax due.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an informal sector makes the tax base an uncertain estimate
questions.stem: A finance committee asks the architect to explain, for the civic complex brief, why a large informal sector complicates the measurement of a country's tax effort.

answer.exemplar: Revenue effort compares tax revenue with the tax base, and the tax base is easier to see than the activity generating it. When a large part of output is produced by businesses that are small, unregistered or run as household enterprises, their output is estimated rather than recorded, and estimates of it vary widely between statisticians. Any figure for the base is therefore uncertain, and the same revenue divided by two different base estimates gives two different rates. The country can therefore appear to have high effort because its informal activity is invisible, or low effort because it is counted generously, without anything having changed in the behaviour of taxpayers.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate explains how an uncertain base contaminates any rate computed from it. A strong answer shows the same revenue yielding different effort figures under different base estimates.
questions.hint: Ask how reliable the denominator is.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish administrative reach from effective service coverage
questions.stem: An architect's brief for rural clinics notes that the health office sends nurses to 84 per cent of settlements but cannot verify that the medicines they carry arrived.

options.text: Capacity is high, because the office reaches most settlements with trained staff
options.misconception: judges capacity by staffing and reach alone

options.text: Capacity is limited, because reaching settlements without reliable supply is not effective coverage
Capacity is high, because the office has an established network of outreach workers
options.misconception: treats an established structure as working capacity

options.text: Capacity cannot be judged, because the brief gives no measure of settlements' population
options.misconception: demands population figures the question does not need

questions.explanation: Administrative capacity is not just offices and personnel but the ability to deliver reliably. Staff reaching settlements without confirmed supplies make contact, not coverage, so reach overstates real capacity.
questions.hint: Ask what reaching a settlement actually delivers.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of posts filled through competitive examination
questions.stem: A brief table compares appointment routes for 240 public housing posts: 162 filled by written examination, 54 by nomination from serving officials and 24 left vacant.

options.text: The merit rule is working, because 162 out of 240 appointments were made by examination
options.misconception: judges the rule by its largest category alone

options.text: The merit rule is failing, because 54 appointments were still made by nomination
options.misconception: declares failure without setting a threshold

options.text: Examination fills about 68 per cent of posts, so a substantial minority still enters without the test
The merit rule cannot be assessed, because the table does not say who chose the examiners
options.misconception: demands detail the table does not need

questions.explanation: 162 of 240 is about 68 per cent, so examination is the main route but not the only one. A merit rule concerns how posts are filled, so the remaining nominations and vacancies still count against it.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the presence of institutions from working state capacity
questions.stem: A draft brief notes that the region has good roads, a trained civil service and functioning courts, yet cannot collect tax from a large informal economy.

options.text: The region has high capacity, because roads, staff and courts are the classic components of it
options.misconception: treats the components as proof of working capacity

options.text: The region has no capacity, because a failure to collect tax shows the administration cannot act
options.misconception: judges the whole by a single failure

options.text: The region has high capacity, because the informal economy is outside the administration's remit
options.misconception: treats a formal remit as full reach

options.text: Capacity is uneven, since the machinery exists but its reach into the informal economy does not

questions.explanation: State capacity is the ability to reach and deliver, not the mere presence of institutions. Roads, a trained service and courts are the instruments, but if they miss most of the economy, capacity falls short.
questions.hint: Ask whether the machinery reaches where people live.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why revenue effort is hard to compare across regions
questions.stem: The architect's brief must explain why comparing revenue effort across two regions is difficult even when their revenue figures are known.

options.text: Because the tax base is estimated differently in each region, so the same revenue gives different rates
Because regions differ in their tax rates, so effort cannot be compared at all
options.misconception: treats rate differences as making comparison impossible

options.text: Because revenue effort only becomes meaningful over a ten-year period of stable collection
options.misconception: invents a time requirement the concept does not have

options.text: Because effort is meaningless unless the region has no informal economy at all
options.misconception: makes informality the condition for the concept to apply

questions.explanation: Revenue effort depends on the base, an estimate whose method differs between regions. The same revenue can show different effort because one counts informal output generously and the other does not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret reported payment behaviour as evidence about tax morale

stimulus.body: We asked 620 registered traders in the district two questions: whether they had voluntarily paid the full business levy last year, and whether they would report a neighbour who did not. Forty-one per cent said they had paid in full without being chased. Of those, 68 per cent said the reason was that they believed the levy was fair and that others were paying it. Among the 59 per cent who had not paid in full, only 12 per cent said they would report a neighbour. A district officer noted that the visible case selection for enforcement has fallen for two years running.

questions.stem: A trader survey is quoted in the architect's brief; the extract is reproduced below.

options.text: The findings show that enforcement has no effect, since the number of reported cases has fallen
options.misconception: reads a fall in visible cases as an absence of deterrence

options.text: Payment tracks belief in fairness more than threat, so effort depends on the levy being seen as legitimate
The findings show that most traders are evading, since only 41 per cent paid in full
options.misconception: reads voluntary payment as evidence of widespread evasion

options.text: The findings show that traders should be given more notice before payment is due
options.misconception: draws an administrative remedy from an attitudinal survey

questions.explanation: Belief that the levy is fair predicts voluntary payment far better than fear of detection, which is tax morale at work. A falling caseload may reflect less reporting rather than more compliance.
questions.hint: Ask which factor explains voluntary payment.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the revenue shortfall from the compliance gap
questions.stem: A budget committee asks the architect to explain, for the civic complex brief, how the compliance gap differs from the revenue shortfall.

answer.exemplar: The revenue shortfall is simply the distance between what the budget expected and what was collected, and it can be closed by collection or by additional receipts. The compliance gap is the part of that shortfall that reflects a deliberate decision not to pay, and it is measured by comparing tax legally due on the declared and detectably understated base with tax actually collected. The difference matters because a gap caused by evasion points at the willingness of taxpayers and at the design of the rules, whereas a shortfall caused by late payment or weak administration points at the collection system. Treatment follows from that difference.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate distinguishes the arithmetical shortfall from the part caused by evasion. A strong answer ties each cause to the remedy that fits it.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the shortfall reflects choice.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an unregistered sector makes the tax base an estimate
questions.stem: A regional note in the brief observes that the district's informal economy produces roughly a fifth of output and that few of those businesses hold registrations.

options.text: The tax base is unaffected, because informal output is not taxed at all
options.misconception: assumes an untaxed sector leaves the base unchanged

options.text: The tax base is unaffected, because the output is still recorded in national accounts
options.misconception: assumes national accounts record informal output precisely

options.text: The tax base is uncertain, because informal output must be estimated rather than registered
The tax base is unchanged, because the government chooses not to tax unregistered activity
options.misconception: treats a policy choice as an absence of activity

questions.explanation: A tax base built from registration counts only visible firms, so a large unregistered sector makes the base an estimate with real error. That uncertainty propagates into any ratio computed from it.
questions.hint: Ask how the base is counted, not what is taxed.

options.misconception: judges capacity by the best performing service

options.text: The district has low capacity, because no service is delivered to a majority of clients
options.misconception: applies a single threshold across different services

options.misconception: counts the variety of services as working capacity

options.text: The office is unevenly effective, with strong routine services and weak ones that need records

questions.explanation: Service reach varies sharply, from 91 per cent on the registry to 38 per cent on land records. A single label for capacity hides that, and the weaker services depend on records kept over time.

questions.topic: Features and consequences of a merit rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain the predictability and contestability a merit rule creates
questions.stem: An architect's brief for a housing programme notes that 240 posts are advertised, tested by written examination and filled from a published ranking, with appeals heard by an independent panel.

options.text: The design makes entry predictable and contestable, since candidates can see the route and challenge it
The design makes entry predictable but contestable only for candidates who can afford a lawyer
options.misconception: assumes appeal depends on private resources

options.text: The design removes discretion, since an examination leaves no room for judgement at all
options.misconception: claims rules eliminate discretion entirely

options.text: The design reduces the quality of appointments, because examinations test knowledge rather than judgement
options.misconception: assumes examination excludes the qualities posts need

questions.explanation: A merit rule's value lies in its visible procedure: a published test, ranking and independent appeal make entry predictable and contestable. It bounds discretion rather than removing judgement.
questions.hint: Ask what a candidate can do if the process is misapplied.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of households reached by a civil register

questions.explanation: 9,600 out of 12,000 is 0.8, that is 80 per cent of households. Such reach is one component of state capacity, since an administration cannot tax or serve people it has no record of.

questions.topic: Fiscal capacity and the tax ratio
questions.learningObjective: Recommend what evidence to read alongside a district's tax ratio
questions.stem: The architect's brief must advise a donor on how to judge the district's fiscal capacity from its public accounts.

options.text: Look at the tax ratio alone, since the take relative to output settles the question
options.misconception: treats one ratio as a complete test

options.text: Look at the ratio, the reliability of collection and the cost of borrowing, since capacity is about resources actually available
Look at the size of the public workforce, since staff numbers reveal whether the state can deliver anything
options.misconception: uses staffing as a proxy for fiscal capacity

options.text: Look at the growth of public investment, since a rising capital programme is proof of healthy finances
options.misconception: reads capital spending as evidence of fiscal health

questions.explanation: Fiscal capacity is the real ability to raise and spend, and a low tax ratio can reflect weak collection or a narrow base. Accounts must be read alongside collection reliability and borrowing costs.
questions.hint: Ask what the ratio leaves out of the picture.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Show how a difference in the estimated base changes a computed effort rate

stimulus.body: Two regions report similar revenue and appear to have similar effort. Region A collected 15,000,000 units and estimated its tax base at 100,000,000 units. Region B collected 12,000,000 units and estimated its tax base at 50,000,000 units. A research team using household surveys put Region B's base at 70,000,000 rather than 50,000,000, on the grounds that the official estimate missed household enterprises. Region B's authorities maintain that the official base reflects the registrable sector only, and argue that the unregistrable remainder is not a tax base at all.

questions.stem: A note attached to the brief compares two regions on revenue and apparent effort.

options.text: Region A has the higher revenue effort, since it collects more money than Region B
options.misconception: compares raw revenue instead of rates

options.text: Region B has the higher revenue effort, and its figure is correct because the official estimate is authoritative
options.misconception: accepts the official base without testing it

options.text: Region B's effort depends on which base is used, since 12 million over 70 million is far below 12 over 50
The comparison cannot be made, because the two regions use different currency units
options.misconception: invents a unit difference the note does not mention

questions.explanation: Region A's effort is 15 per cent; Region B's is 24 per cent on 50 million but about 17 per cent on 70 million. The comparison turns on an estimate of the base, which is what makes it fragile.
questions.hint: Compute both rates for Region B.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why progressive burdens tend to support tax morale
questions.stem: A municipal partner asks the architect to explain, for the civic complex brief, why tax morale tends to be higher where the burden appears to fall on those who earn most.

answer.exemplar: Tax morale is the willingness to pay what is owed, and it depends on whether the taxpayer believes the arrangement is fair. Progressivity, where those with larger incomes pay a larger share, supports that belief because the tax is visibly linked to ability to pay and because evasion by the better off is easy to observe. Where the visible burden appears to fall on the majority while the wealthy are treated leniently, the same rule reads as unjust, and people come to see paying as optional. The policy implication is that a progressive rate is not merely redistributive: it changes the terms on which compliance is judged, and so it changes how much is collected voluntarily rather than through enforcement.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate connects the fairness of the burden to willingness to pay rather than describing progressivity. A strong answer traces the mechanism from visible burden to compliance.
questions.hint: Ask why the same rule can be judged fair or unfair.

options.text: The evaded portion is 700,000 units, with the remainder under appeal rather than necessarily evaded

questions.explanation: Tax due less tax collected is 700,000, but that includes amounts contested on appeal. The part that is evasion rather than dispute is not the whole gap, so the two differ.
questions.hint: Separate disputed amounts from amounts evaded.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Fiscal capacity and the tax ratio
questions.learningObjective: Judge fiscal capacity from a tax ratio, collection rates and borrowing costs

stimulus.body: The district's budget documents show total tax revenue of 42,000,000 units against an estimated output of 500,000,000 units, a ratio of 8.4 per cent. A separate note from the finance office records that collection of the property levy has been running at 88 per cent of the amount billed for three years, and that the district has refinanced its hospital debt twice in five years at interest rates between 9 and 13 per cent. The municipality has no formal borrowing ceiling, and the office notes that it has not needed one because lenders have continued to offer terms.

questions.stem: A budget extract in the brief shows the district's tax revenue and output as recorded below.

options.text: Fiscal capacity looks secure, since the ratio of 8.4 per cent is above the regional average of seven
options.misconception: compares with an average without examining collection or debt

options.text: Fiscal capacity looks secure, since lenders continue to offer terms on the district's debt
options.misconception: treats continued access to credit as proof of strength

options.text: Fiscal capacity looks weak, since the property levy is collected at only 88 per cent of the amount billed
options.misconception: reads one collection shortfall as decisive on its own

options.text: Fiscal capacity is mixed, since the take looks reasonable but collection gaps and costly debt limit what is usable

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the estimated tax base conditions any revenue effort rate
questions.stem: A statistician asks the architect to explain, for the civic complex brief, why revenue effort must be read alongside the way the tax base is estimated.

answer.exemplar: Revenue effort is a ratio, and its denominator is not observed but constructed. The base is typically assembled from business registrations, wage records and estimates of informal output, and those estimates differ between statistical offices and between years. When the base is revised upward, the same unchanged revenue produces a lower effort figure, and the movement is an artefact of the estimate rather than any change in taxpayer behaviour. Revenue effort is therefore useful for describing the revenue that is actually collected, but it should not be used as a performance measure of the administration or the compliance of taxpayers without that qualification.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate explains the estimating step behind the denominator rather than only defining the ratio. A strong answer shows a base revision moving the rate with no change in behaviour.
questions.hint: Ask how the denominator is produced.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Fiscal capacity and the tax ratio
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two districts with the same tax ratio can differ in fiscal capacity
questions.stem: A regional finance group asks the architect to explain, for the civic complex brief, why two districts with the same tax ratio can have very different fiscal capacity.

answer.exemplar: The tax ratio compares revenue with output, so it can hide where the money actually goes. A district with a high ratio but a very narrow base, heavy borrowing costs and a large unfunded wage bill has less room to act than one with a lower ratio spread across a wide base and cheap credit. The ratio also says nothing about how reliably the revenue is collected: a district that bills aggressively and collects late has revenue on paper and cash shortages in practice. Fiscal capacity therefore has to be judged from the ratio together with the breadth of the base, the reliability of collection and the cost of financing, since what matters to a government building or operating a facility is the money it can actually commit.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate treats the tax ratio as one input rather than a verdict. A strong answer names the other dimensions and why each changes what a government can commit.
questions.hint: Ask what the ratio cannot reveal.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why state capacity is not the same as the size of the public administration
questions.stem: A consultant asks the architect to explain, for the civic complex brief, why state capacity should not be described simply as the size of the public administration.

answer.exemplar: The size of the public administration counts posts, not results. A large civil service can be concentrated in offices that few citizens reach, spending most of its effort on internal coordination, while a smaller one can deliver registration, licensing and payments accurately to most households. Capacity is about what the administration can actually reach and deliver reliably across the territory, so it has to be judged from outcomes such as the share of households registered, the share of permits issued within the statutory period, and the share of declared liability collected. Staff numbers are an input that may or may not turn into those outcomes, and the architecture of a district's services depends on which it is.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate distinguishes administrative inputs from delivered capacity. A strong answer ties capacity to measurable reach and reliability rather than to headcount.
questions.hint: Ask what the posts produce, not how many there are.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Features and consequences of a merit rule
questions.learningObjective: State what a merit rule governs and what lies outside its scope
questions.stem: A housing committee asks the architect to explain, for the civic complex brief, what a merit rule changes and what it leaves unchanged.

answer.exemplar: A merit rule changes how entry happens: posts are advertised, candidates are tested on a published instrument, shortlists and results are published, and unsuccessful candidates can obtain reasons and appeal. That removes the discretion to select on personal ties and makes the outcome predictable to those preparing for it. It leaves several things unchanged. It does not decide how many posts should exist, it does not guarantee that the test measures what the job needs, it does not guarantee that the selected candidate performs well once appointed, and it does not affect the informal influences that surround a post after it has been filled. It is one rule about entry, and its effects should not be overstated beyond that.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate says what a merit rule governs and what lies outside it. A strong answer separates selection from staffing levels, test design and later performance.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule does not decide.

options.misconception: presumes base widening would touch the evading taxpayers

options.text: Apply a general amnesty, since forgiving past arrears is the fairest response to a large gap
options.misconception: treats forgiveness as necessarily fair to non-payers

options.text: Target the specific tax with audit and registration checks, since the gap is concentrated and diagnosable
Lower the rate on that tax, since a lower rate would make evasion less attractive to firms
options.misconception: assumes evasion responds only to the size of the rate

questions.explanation: A gap concentrated in one tax is diagnosable, and targeted instruments work on it: registration checks, audits where invoices are inflated. Widening the base addresses something else.
questions.hint: Ask where the missing money is concentrated.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare two ways of estimating a tax base and their weaknesses

stimulus.body: The finance office calculates revenue effort in two ways. Under the first, the tax base is registered turnover only, which gives the district a base of 40,000,000 units and a ratio of 10 per cent. Under the second, the office adds a labour force estimate of 120,000 workers each assumed to produce 1,000 units of output per year, giving a base of 160,000,000 units and a ratio of 2.5 per cent. The office publishes the second figure as the headline because registered turnover omits much of what the district produces. A reviewer notes that the labour force estimate was carried over unchanged from a survey conducted seven years earlier.

questions.stem: A method note in the brief calculates revenue effort two ways; it is reproduced below.

options.text: The district should publish the first ratio, because the larger base overstates the district's taxable capacity
options.misconception: prefers the narrower base without a stated reason

options.text: The two ratios show that revenue collection is weak, since they differ so greatly from one another
options.misconception: reads a difference between estimates as evidence about collection

options.text: The second ratio is preferable, since including all output gives a truer picture of the district's activity
options.misconception: accepts a stale estimate because the method is broader

options.text: Neither ratio should stand alone, since one ignores most output and the other relies on a seven-year-old estimate

questions.explanation: The first base ignores most informal production; the second relies on a labour estimate seven years old. Publishing either alone risks a wrong conclusion, so method and vintage should be shown.
questions.hint: Ask what each estimate depends on.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why capacity must be assessed where services are hardest to deliver
questions.stem: A regional planner asks the architect to explain, for the civic complex brief, why administrative capacity has to be assessed alongside the reach of services into poor and remote areas.

answer.exemplar: Capacity measured only in the places where the administration already works will look strong even where services never arrive. Poor and remote settlements typically carry the costs of distance, thin staffing and irregular revenue, so they are the places where a service is most likely to be a paper exercise rather than a functioning one. Measuring reach into these areas therefore shows whether the administration can act on its stated intentions everywhere, not only where it is convenient. For a programme building clinics, schools or water connections, that difference decides whether the facility is used or merely recorded, since a service that does not reach the people it was meant for leaves the underlying condition untouched and consumes the capital that was supposed to relieve it.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate explains why an average reach figure conceals the areas that matter most. A strong answer connects where capacity is measured with whether services function where needed.
questions.hint: Ask where the measurement is taken.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Features and consequences of a merit rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an out-of-date test undermines a merit rule
questions.stem: An architect's brief for a district recruitment policy notes that the published examination syllabus was revised three years ago and has not been updated since.

options.text: A stale syllabus weakens the rule, since the test no longer matches the work the post involves
A stale syllabus strengthens the rule, because continuity in the test makes results comparable over time
options.misconception: treats continuity as automatically valuable

options.text: A stale syllabus strengthens the rule, because candidates can prepare for a familiar instrument
options.misconception: confuses candidate convenience with selection quality

options.text: A stale syllabus has no effect, since the published rules matter more than what the test measures
options.misconception: assumes procedure alone determines fitness

questions.explanation: A merit rule works by matching the test to the work, so an out-of-date instrument selects for the wrong qualities while appearing rigorous. Aligning the test with the post preserves its value.
questions.hint: Ask what the test actually measures now.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read variation in state reach across functions as uneven capacity
questions.stem: A brief table records state reach across five functions: births registered 98 per cent, driving licences issued 94, land titles regularised 71, business permits granted 46 and sewage connections billed 39.

options.text: The state is uniformly strong, because every function exceeds one third of its target population
options.misconception: applies a low uniform threshold to functions with different targets

options.text: Capacity is uneven, strong on personal registration and weak on services requiring land and business records
The state is weak overall, because the mean of the five figures is below seventy per cent
options.misconception: averages away the variation that matters

options.text: The state is weak overall, because the two lowest figures concern the newest functions
options.misconception: invents an age ranking the table does not record

questions.explanation: Functions needing standing records sit at 71 per cent and below, while personal registration reaches 94 and 98. Capacity is strong where transactions are simple and weak where records come first.
questions.hint: Ask which functions depend on records held in advance.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Fiscal capacity and the tax ratio
questions.learningObjective: Compute a tax ratio and state what the ratio does not show
questions.stem: An architect's brief notes that a district's tax revenue of 3,150,000 units sits on estimated output of 45,000,000 units.

options.text: The tax ratio is 14 per cent, so the district's revenue effort is among the highest recorded
options.misconception: misdivides the figures when computing the ratio

options.text: The tax ratio is 7 per cent, which places the district above the regional average of six
options.misconception: compares with an average the brief does not supply

options.text: The tax ratio is 7 per cent, describing the take without showing how reliably it is collected
The tax ratio cannot be computed, because estimated output is not a measured quantity
options.misconception: refuses to work with an estimated denominator at all

questions.explanation: 3,150,000 over 45,000,000 is 0.07, that is 7 per cent. The ratio describes the take against the size of the economy and says nothing about how reliably the revenue is collected.
questions.hint: Divide revenue by output and multiply by 100.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate revenue effort and state the condition attached to the rate
questions.stem: An architect's brief records tax revenue of 3,150,000 units for a district with an estimated tax base of 45,000,000 units. What is the revenue effort as a percentage of the base?
questions.explanation: 3,150,000 over 45,000,000 is 0.07, that is 7 per cent. The figure is useful only against its base, since a base revised upward would produce a lower rate from exactly the same revenue collected.
questions.hint: Divide revenue by the estimated tax base.
